source_refs.note: Book p. 41-42: 2.5 Derivative of Exponential Functions, Recall! box, derivation of d/dx(a^x), Challenge! box, Example 7

blocks.text:
A function defined by
\[f(x) = a^{x},\]
where \(a > 0\) and \(a \ne 1\), is called an exponential function.
If \(a = e \approx 2.71828\), then \(f(x) = e^{x}\) is called the natural exponential function.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
In \(a^{x}\) the variable \(x\) is in the power and the base \(a\) is a fixed number. Compare \(x^{3}\) (variable base, fixed power: a power function) with \(3^{x}\) (fixed base, variable power: an exponential function). They are differentiated by completely different rules, so first decide which kind you have.
Why \(a > 0\) and \(a \ne 1\)? For \(a = 1\), \(1^{x} = 1\) is just a constant. For \(a < 0\), values such as \((-4)^{1/2}\) are not real numbers.
The number \(e \approx 2.71828\) is special because, as we will see below, \(e^{x}\) is its own derivative.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
This standard limit is the key to the whole derivation, so take it as known. A quick numerical feel for it with \(a = 2\) and \(h = 0.001\):
\[\dfrac{2^{0.001} - 1}{0.001} \approx 0.6934\]
\[\ln 2 \approx 0.6931\]
The smaller \(h\) is, the closer the two numbers get.

Now, we shall find the derivative of \(f(x) = a^{x}\), using the definition.
Let
\[f(x) = a^{x} \quad \text{...(1)}\]
From equation (1) we have
\[f(x + h) = a^{x + h} \quad \text{...(2)}\]
\[f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}\]
(definition of derivative)

After substituting the expression for \(f(x)\) and \(f(x + h)\) from equations (1) and (2), we get:
\[f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{a^{x + h} - a^{x}}{h}\]
\[= \lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{a^{x}(a^{h} - 1)}{h}\]
\[= a^{x} \lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{a^{h} - 1}{h}\]
\[= a^{x} \ln a\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
What happened in each line:
1. Law of exponents: \(a^{x + h} = a^{x} \cdot a^{h}\), so \(a^{x}\) is a common factor of the numerator.
2. The limit is taken as \(h \to 0\); \(a^{x}\) does not contain \(h\), so it behaves like a constant and comes outside the limit.
3. The limit that is left is exactly the Recall! result, \(\ln a\).

blocks.title: Challenge!
blocks.text:
Prove that \(\frac{d}{dx}(e^{x}) = e^{x}\).
Do you know \(\ln e = 1\)?

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Answer to the Challenge (our working). \(\ln e = \log_{e} e = 1\), because \(e^{1} = e\). Put \(a = e\) in the boxed result:
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}(e^{x}) = e^{x} \ln e\]
\[= e^{x} \cdot 1 = e^{x}\]
So \(e^{x}\) is its own derivative; this is why \(e\) is the natural base.
With the Chain Rule (2.3), if \(u\) is a function of \(x\):
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}(e^{u}) = e^{u}\,\dfrac{du}{dx}\]
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}(a^{u}) = a^{u} \ln a\,\dfrac{du}{dx}\]
These two forms are used in Example 7 and in Exercise 2.2.

blocks.title: Example 7
steps:
Given: (i) \(y = e^{\sin^{2} x}\); (ii) \(y = a^{x^{3}}\).
To find: \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) in each part.
Method: both are exponentials whose power is itself a function of \(x\), so we use the Chain Rule forms \(\frac{d}{dx}(e^{u}) = e^{u}\frac{du}{dx}\) and \(\frac{d}{dx}(a^{u}) = a^{u}\ln a\,\frac{du}{dx}\).

(i) Step 1: Chain Rule on the outer exponential
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = e^{\sin^{2} x}\,\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin^{2} x)\]
Why: here \(u = \sin^{2} x\). The exponential is copied unchanged and multiplied by the derivative of its power.

(i) Step 2: Differentiate \(\sin^{2} x = (\sin x)^{2}\)
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin x)^{2} = 2\sin x\,\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin x)\]
\[= 2\sin x \cos x\]
Why: power rule with the Chain Rule again (inner function \(\sin x\)), and \(\frac{d}{dx}(\sin x) = \cos x\) from 2.2.

(i) Step 3: Put it together
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = e^{\sin^{2} x} \cdot 2\sin x \cos x\]
\[= 2\sin x \cos x\, e^{\sin^{2} x}\]
Why: the book writes the factors in front of the exponential. (Optionally \(2\sin x\cos x = \sin 2x\).)

(ii) Step 1: Chain Rule for base \(a\)
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = a^{x^{3}} \ln a\,\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^{3})\]
Why: here \(u = x^{3}\); for base \(a\) the extra factor \(\ln a\) appears, from \(\frac{d}{dx}(a^{u}) = a^{u}\ln a\,\frac{du}{dx}\).

(ii) Step 2: Finish
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = a^{x^{3}} \ln a\,(3x^{2})\]
\[= 3x^{2} a^{x^{3}} \ln a\]
Why: power rule \(\frac{d}{dx}(x^{3}) = 3x^{2}\); then the factors are rearranged.

Check:
(i) at \(x = 0\): \(\frac{dy}{dx} = 2(0)(1)e^{0} = 0\). This fits: \(\sin^{2} x\) has its smallest value 0 at \(x = 0\), so \(y\) has a minimum there and the slope is 0.
(ii) with \(a = e\): \(y = e^{x^{3}}\) and the formula gives \(3x^{2}e^{x^{3}}\) because \(\ln e = 1\), the same as the \(e^{u}\) rule gives directly.
blocks.answer: (i) \(\frac{dy}{dx} = 2\sin x \cos x\, e^{\sin^{2} x}\) (ii) \(\frac{dy}{dx} = 3x^{2} a^{x^{3}} \ln a\)

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text:
'Copy, then multiply': to differentiate \(e^{(\text{anything})}\), copy \(e^{(\text{anything})}\) unchanged and multiply by the derivative of the anything. For \(a^{(\text{anything})}\), also multiply by \(\ln a\).
Always say which rule you are using (Chain Rule); examiners give marks for the method line.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Exponential function: \(f(x) = a^{x}\), \(a > 0\), \(a \ne 1\); natural exponential: \(e^{x}\), \(e \approx 2.71828\).
2. \(\frac{d}{dx}(a^{x}) = a^{x}\ln a\), proved from the definition using \(\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{a^{h} - 1}{h} = \ln a\).
3. \(\frac{d}{dx}(e^{x}) = e^{x}\), since \(\ln e = 1\).
4. Chain Rule forms: \(\frac{d}{dx}(e^{u}) = e^{u}u'\) and \(\frac{d}{dx}(a^{u}) = a^{u}\ln a\,u'\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Using the power rule on an exponential: \(\frac{d}{dx}(2^{x}) \ne x\,2^{x-1}\). The correct answer is \(2^{x}\ln 2\).
2. Forgetting the derivative of the power: \(\frac{d}{dx}(e^{\sin^{2} x})\) is not just \(e^{\sin^{2} x}\).
3. Forgetting \(\ln a\) when the base is not \(e\), or writing \(\ln a\) when the base is \(e\) (it is 1 there).
